author: Alex Berger
title: Russian national to appear in Albany court for allegedly violating export laws - NewsBreak
text:
By Alex Berger ,
1 hours ago ALBANY, N.Y. ( WTEN ) -- The Federal Bureau of Investigation announced that a Russian man living in Sweden, who ran an electronics company in Hong Kong, will stand before a judge in Albany.
Download our WTEN+ streaming app on Roku, Fire TV and Apple TV! 50-year-old Alexander Suvorov is a Russian citizen who managed a Hong Kong based electronics company called GS Group. Suvorov had never set foot in the United States until being extradited to New York's Northern District, after law enforcement said he tried to send components for electronics like drones, weapon platforms and radars to Russia, using shell companies as a front.
He would allegedly circumvent Export Administration Regulations outlined by the U.S. Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) to plan and act with other people to send the electronic components to Russia.

"Our responsibility is to detect the threats early, follow the evidence wherever it leads, and work with our partners to stop criminal activities before they turn into national security emergencies," said Craig Tremaroli, special agent in charge of the FBI Albany Field Office. "That's what we did here."
Suvorov faces three different charges here in the states including conspiring in money laundering, outbound smuggling and violating export laws.
How the FBI tracked down Suvorov FBI Special Agent Carson Walker filed a criminal complaint in Aug. 2025, saying there was probable cause to say Suvorov had conspired with people "known and unknown" to "transport, transmit, and transfer a monetary instrument and funds to a place in the United States from and through a place outside the United States, with the intent to promote the carrying on of specified unlawful activity."
Three people outlined in the complaint, Suvorov, Infotechnika Employee 1 and NPC Topaz Director 1 are the parties accused of participating in the fraudulent "network" federal officials outlined.
Infotechnika, an electronics company based in Saint Petersburg, Russia, had the same physical address as NPO Electronic Systems. NPO was added to the BIS Entity List , which outlines companies that have to have specific license requirements for export, re-export or in-country transferring of "controlled items," so that "sensitive technologies do not fall into the hands of those who would threaten U.S. national security or American citizens."
NPO was added to the BIS Entity List in March 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine because the company had been "involved in, contributed to, or otherwise supported the Russian security services, military and defense sectors, and military or defense research and development efforts," according to Special Agent Walker.
Amid the of several instances of illegal activity outlined by federal officials, in Oct. 2022 Suvorov had emailed a Hong Kong based business services company.
Suvorov had created a new company called Unitech Impex Ltd and was inquiring about opening a bank account. In April of 2023, a questionnaire sent by Suvorov to the Hong Kong based company had Suvorov listed as the only director, shareholder, ultimate beneficial owner and bank account signatory.
The questionnaire also included that Suvorov got his income from selling electronic components. It also said there was a U.S. company as a supplier and two Russian companies as buyers.
Suvorov told the company based in Hong Kong that Unitech would be a supplier for a buyer in Russia, and opening the bank account would "separate the business with Russia into one distinct flow," and would make it "easy to close one company...without influence to the whole business, which is not connected to Russia."
Special Agent Walker then asked for an arrest warrant for Suvorov after discovering this exchange, along with the other illegal activity Suvorov allegedly was a part of.
But, the FBI got a break in the case when Suvorov tried to buy parts to sell to Russia from a business here in the Northern District.
"That company reported it wisely," said John Sarcone III, first assistant U.S. attorney of the Northern District of New York. "See something, say something. They would have potentially been a victim. That's how we were able to obtain jurisdiction."
Suvorov will appear in Albany court tomorrow afternoon.
